<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0598c1bb5aa61a76">Why reduce only positive high-tail-risk credit?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ataco">TACO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johns Hopkins University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Correct trajectories can contain unlikely, unsound steps. Reduce their positive reinforcement smoothly while retaining negative signals for failures. Contextual risk is not a low-probability equals wrong rule; no real local predictor.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A lucky correct guess needn&#x27;t be rewarded as strongly, but its negative feedback in a failed trajectory remains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07976">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2607.07976-taco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0598c1bb5aa61a76">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:taco" data-paper-title="TACO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-3393248b5a7d48c9">Does TACO scale positive and negative advantages the same way?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ataco">TACO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johns Hopkins University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Reduce positive credit only for high-risk tokens, leaving nonpositive advantages unchanged. This preserves failure learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A rare word in a failed response should not escape the original penalty solely for high risk.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07976">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2607.07976-taco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3393248b5a7d48c9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:taco" data-paper-title="TACO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ae3e76c30e78f7d">Does local TACO reproduce a contextual tail-risk predictor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ataco">TACO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johns Hopkins University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Candidate actions verify credit direction, not long-CoT token risk. Smooth weights must be between zero and one; don&#x27;t simply delete all unlikely tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A supplied risk label tests branching, not automatic detection of implausibility.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07976">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2607.07976-taco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ae3e76c30e78f7d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:scar-shapley-credit" data-paper-title="SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-scar-shapley-credit-01c57925" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4ac7a70be0008147">Why consider coalitional marginal contributions of spans in SCAR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ascar-shapley-credit">SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · McGill University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A span&#x27;s value depends on other spans. Shapley weights gains over coalitions to allocate terminal reward, including negative contributions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An explanation can help only when its premise is also present.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20417v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2505.20417-scar-shapley-credit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4ac7a70be0008147">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:scar-shapley-credit" data-paper-title="SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-933b9e934b9cdf0b">Why retain negative Shapley values and credit only the span&#x27;s final token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ascar-shapley-credit">SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · McGill University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A span may reduce frozen RM value, so clipping breaks decomposition. End-token placement and original-order coalitions define reward scattering. Total equivalence has discount conditions; small exact enumeration isn&#x27;t Owen approximation or full RLHF.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A contradictory extra paragraph can reduce value; zeroing its negative credit breaks total equality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20417v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2505.20417-scar-shapley-credit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-933b9e934b9cdf0b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:scar-shapley-credit" data-paper-title="SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-616c8387b8bbd255">How does the exact local Shapley component differ from the paper&#x27;s SHAP/Owen pipeline?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ascar-shapley-credit">SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · McGill University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Enumeration is exponential and accepts small complete value tables only. The full method also has adaptive segmentation and hierarchical approximation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three spans permit all coalitions; dozens of spans do not fit the same budget.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20417v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2505.20417-scar-shapley-credit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-616c8387b8bbd255">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:scar-shapley-credit" data-paper-title="SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a9863037678e5668">Why place SCAR credit at span end and preserve masked positions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ascar-shapley-credit">SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · McGill University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Score coalitions in original order, filling excluded positions with spaces, and assign credit to each span&#x27;s last token. Keep negatives and zero empty value. Reward conservation requires the corresponding γ=1 condition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Joining text across removed middle spans changes the defined coalition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20417v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2505.20417-scar-shapley-credit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a9863037678e5668">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:intuitor" data-paper-title="INTUITOR" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-intuitor-7b64d1c3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-74312e0a24ed0414">Where does INTUITOR reward come from without an external verifier?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aintuitor">INTUITOR</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compute self-certainty from each prefix&#x27;s full next-token distribution and average across the response. This is intrinsic signal, not correctness; use independent evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A sharp distribution can still produce wrong arithmetic.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19590">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2505.19590-intuitor/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-74312e0a24ed0414">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:intuitor" data-paper-title="INTUITOR" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-601f1127c7c740bf">Can negative entropy replace INTUITOR self-certainty?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aintuitor">INTUITOR</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The paper uses KL(U||p), unlike KL(p||U) or negative entropy; low-probability tails affect directions differently. Local sampled-candidate ratios aren&#x27;t tokenwise reproduction. Confidence isn&#x27;t correctness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two distributions with similar maxima can have very different small tails, which KL directions weight differently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19590">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2505.19590-intuitor/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-601f1127c7c740bf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:intuitor" data-paper-title="INTUITOR" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-353bedaefa0b55ce">Can INTUITOR&#x27;s intrinsic KL and reference KL be merged?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aintuitor">INTUITOR</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Uniform-to-current KL measures certainty; reference KL anchors drift. They use different references and roles. Treating intrinsic reward as regularization changes the target.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One encourages certainty while another discourages moving from old policy, potentially opposing each other.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19590">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2505.19590-intuitor/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-353bedaefa0b55ce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:intuitor" data-paper-title="INTUITOR" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-48559647056aa759">Does current intuitor code implement full-vocabulary self-certainty?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aintuitor">INTUITOR</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Reward uses sampled-candidate logp+log N and diagnostic KL(p||U), lacking token-level full-vocabulary KL(U||p). Historical scores remain diagnostics even if docs are corrected.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Changing the documented direction does not alter the executable branch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19590">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2505.19590-intuitor/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-48559647056aa759">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:math-shepherd" data-paper-title="Math-Shepherd" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-math-shepherd-cc3174ec" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4aa9a43e201b22c1">How does Math-Shepherd get step supervision without human step labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Amath-shepherd">Math-Shepherd</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Continue repeatedly from a prefix and estimate reachable success from final answer checks, then train a process verifier. This is not direct human judgment of each line.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A prefix with mostly correct continuations receives a higher success estimate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2312.08935-math-shepherd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4aa9a43e201b22c1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:math-shepherd" data-paper-title="Math-Shepherd" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-162d99ef25d3753e">Why isn&#x27;t a continuation-based step label a direct correctness judgment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Amath-shepherd">Math-Shepherd</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It estimates success under a particular policy and sampling budget. Correct prefixes can get low estimates and wrong ones can be repaired. Separate reachability from correctness; use gold only for annotation or independent scoring.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Low success after a correct second step may reflect frequent final arithmetic mistakes, not a wrong second step.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2312.08935-math-shepherd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-162d99ef25d3753e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:math-shepherd" data-paper-title="Math-Shepherd" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a1b3f74d41607794">How does continuation success differ from correctness of a step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Amath-shepherd">Math-Shepherd</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Later policy can repair an error or fail after correct reasoning. Estimated reachability combines prefix and continuation policy, not a logical proof.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A wrong step followed by frequent corrections should not be imitated simply because continuations succeed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2312.08935-math-shepherd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a1b3f74d41607794">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:math-shepherd" data-paper-title="Math-Shepherd" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">

<h2 id="qa-92344e3f0c9b1409">Can Math-Shepherd continuations see gold when constructing labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Amath-shepherd">Math-Shepherd</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Gold is only for terminal checking; actually sample from the specified prefix rather than constructing a path from known answers. No full local LLM data/PRM training.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:process-supervision" data-paper-title="Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-process-supervision-e0dd1357" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-db9edb2d592cf144">Why do process supervision methods label steps rather than only outcomes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprocess-supervision">Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Failure doesn&#x27;t identify the broken step. Local labels provide finer learning and selection, requiring annotations or reliable process judges. Do not broadcast terminal correctness as step truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If step three fails, steps one and two needn&#x27;t be marked wrong.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2305.20050-process-supervision/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-db9edb2d592cf144">Question link</a></p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:process-supervision" data-paper-title="Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c928a3ae66cbf1b">Why actively label uncertain steps instead of only checking final answers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprocess-supervision">Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Final outcomes don&#x27;t locate early mistakes. Step labels provide detailed reward-model supervision; uncertainty targets current ambiguous decisions but isn&#x27;t a universal error proxy. Control candidate/evaluation budgets; no full local annotation dataset.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Review an uncertain key algebraic move rather than repeatedly labeling obvious format.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:process-supervision" data-paper-title="Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">

<h2 id="qa-14599bd243e344eb">What tradeoff separates active uncertain-step labeling from random labeling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprocess-supervision">Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Active selection spends budget on hard judgments; random selection better reflects the original distribution. Uncertainty isn&#x27;t importance and selection bias/label quality remain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An ambiguous formatting step can be less valuable to review than a key mathematical transition.</p>

<h2 id="qa-fc42fa618967fd6a">How separate PRM labels and predictions?</h2>

<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:concur" data-paper-title="CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-concur-c984323b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-928962c2c93fbd5b">Why can standardized rewards violate primary priority despite gating raw auxiliary rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aconcur">CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The raw gate constrains auxiliary scores for failures. Independent centering/scaling can amplify small auxiliary gaps enough to reverse primary order. At a primary ceiling the primary advantage is zero, so auxiliary can determine the update. CONCUR constrains standardized terms, not just the raw gate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two correct answers differ slightly in length reward. Standardization can give length unit variance while primary advantage is zero; this is not evidence of learning more correct answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36437v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.36437-concur/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-928962c2c93fbd5b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:concur" data-paper-title="CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-aebcbcd2e1c9e89d">Why sort by primary then auxiliary before PAVA without averaging all equal primary scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aconcur">CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Monotonicity only constrains strictly higher primary levels, not equal non-ceiling primary values. Sorting ties by auxiliary lets PAVA fix cross-primary violations only. Equal outputs are required at the ceiling only when that tie is enabled.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Primary [0.3,0.3,0.7], auxiliary [-1,0,1] is already feasible. Replacing the two first values with −0.5 adds a constraint.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地结果与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36437v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.36437-concur/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aebcbcd2e1c9e89d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:concur" data-paper-title="CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2b9aaf1497f68e59">Does CONCUR-A exceeding two standard errors prove auxiliary reliability at the ceiling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aconcur">CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It measures concordance of passing pairs with different primary values, releasing ties after at least 61 valid readings and mean greater than two standard errors. The evolving distribution is not IID, and ceiling pairs are not directly measured. This is not a significance level or universal guarantee.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Concordance can reverse later and drop below the threshold; rebind the ceiling rather than treating the first release as permanent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36437v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.36437-concur/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2b9aaf1497f68e59">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:concur" data-paper-title="CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-471defe083f8036a">Can the first group in a batch decide the CONCUR-A ceiling from only previous history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aconcur">CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Algorithm 1 merges every valid reading in the batch before sharing one policy per task/auxiliary and projecting groups. Sequential updates would depend on group order. Final whitening spans the full multi-task batch, not each group. A tensor check is not LLM lift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: History has 60 valid positives and group two supplies the 61st; group one also uses the merged current trust state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界, 代码映射. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36437v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.36437-concur/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-471defe083f8036a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>

<details class="ar-learning-guide" markdown="1"><summary>Topic guide and reading order</summary>

## Start with this question

How can one final score become a training signal that does not reward wrong steps?

## Takeaway

Reward defines what is good; credit determines which actions receive it. Process supervision labels intermediate steps. Math-Shepherd samples continuations and uses their eventual solvability to construct step labels. Rubrics and multiple objectives must map criteria to tokens and prevent one reward from overpowering another. Outcome rewards, process evidence, and advantages are related but distinct. CONCUR shows that even correctness-gated length rewards can reverse primary-reward order after normalization, motivating an explicit projection constraint rather than only reducing the auxiliary weight.

## Example

A math response can reason well for two steps, make a mistake at step three, and still guess the correct answer. Applying terminal reward to all steps can reinforce the error. Independent continuations or step checks give finer evidence, but a failed continuation may reflect inadequate sampling rather than an incorrect prefix.

## Common pitfall

Judge agreement does not establish truth, and style or shortcuts can manipulate rubric scores. Evaluate label quality, the credit formula, and capability separately. Keep hidden answers inside the evaluator. Synthetic credit checks are not evidence of reasoning, robotics, or video-generation ability.

## Reading order

Read Process Supervision for step versus outcome labels, Math-Shepherd for continuation-based labels, and TACO for why even correct answers can contain tokens that should not be reinforced.

1. [Let's Verify Step by Step](../../../../post-training/2305.20050-process-supervision/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050)
2. [Math-Shepherd](../../../../post-training/2312.08935-math-shepherd/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935)
3. [TACO](../../../../post-training/2607.07976-taco/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07976)

## Check your understanding

If a long answer ends correctly, can uniform positive token credit prove every step was correct?

??? note "Show suggested answer"

    No. Terminal reward says only that the final output met the acceptance condition. Uniform credit is an estimation choice that can reinforce wrong steps. Fine-grained credit likewise needs a reliable source and independent comparisons; a judge score is not process ground truth.

</details>
